title: Highest-Protein Legumes: A Nutrition Ranking

seo.title: Highest-Protein Legumes Ranked
seo.meta_description: Compare cooked soybeans, lentils, beans, chickpeas and peas by protein per 100 grams and per realistic serving.
seo.search_intent: Nutrition ranking of legumes by protein content.

excerpt: Cooked mature soybeans lead common legumes by a wide margin. Lentils, beans and chickpeas typically provide about 8–10 grams per 100 grams cooked, translating to much more in a cup-sized serving.
content_html:
Legumes are unusually useful plant proteins because people eat them by the cup, not by the teaspoon. To rank them fairly, compare cooked legumes with cooked legumes. Dry beans look much higher in protein simply because they have not absorbed cooking water yet.

Cooked legume protein ranking

Cooked legumeApprox. protein/100 g
Mature soybeansabout 18 g
Lentils9.0 g
White beans8–10 g
Kidney/pinto beans8–9 g
Chickpeas8–9 g
Split peasabout 8 g
Green peas5–6 g

Soybeans are the outlier

Mature cooked soybeans provide roughly twice the protein concentration of many cooked beans. Soy also supplies the raw material for tofu, tempeh, soy milk and textured soy protein, each with a different water content and protein density.

Lentils

Cooked lentils provide about 9 g per 100 g. A 200 g serving is roughly 18 g. Dry lentils are around 24–25 g per 100 g, but that is not a contradiction: cooking water increases their weight dramatically.

Beans and chickpeas

Common cooked beans and chickpeas cluster in a similar range. A cup-sized serving can contribute roughly 15–20 g of protein plus a substantial amount of fiber.

Green peas versus split peas

Fresh green peas contain more water and less protein per 100 g. Split peas are mature dried peas and become more protein-dense even after cooking.

Serving size tells the practical story

FoodExample servingApprox. protein
Cooked soybeans150 g27 g
Cooked lentils200 g18 g
Cooked beans200 g16–20 g
Cooked chickpeas200 g16–18 g
Green peas200 g10–12 g

Protein quality

Soy has a particularly strong essential-amino-acid profile. Other legumes are relatively lower in sulfur-containing amino acids, while grains tend to be lower in lysine. A varied diet across the day covers those differences without requiring exact protein pairing at every meal.

Canned versus home-cooked

Canned beans retain protein and fiber well. Sodium may be higher when salt is added to the packing liquid; draining and rinsing can reduce some surface sodium. Compare labels if sodium is important to you.

Frequently asked questions

Which bean has the most protein?

If soybeans are included, mature soybeans are the clear leader. Among common non-soy beans, values are close enough that serving size matters more than small ranking differences.

Do lentils beat chickpeas?

Cooked lentils are often slightly higher in protein per 100 g, but both are meaningful sources.

Are canned beans lower in protein?

Not in a way that makes them poor protein foods. Compare drained product and pay more attention to sodium differences.

faq.question: Which legume has the most protein?
faq.answer: Mature cooked soybeans lead common legumes at roughly 18 g per 100 g.

faq.question: How much protein is in 200 g of cooked lentils?
faq.answer: About 18 g using a representative value of 9 g per 100 g.

faq.question: Should dry and cooked beans be ranked together?
faq.answer: No. Dry beans contain far less water, which inflates nutrients per 100 g compared with cooked beans.
